## D-261 — the interface ships as a FIFTH layer outside the wheel, and turning the type checker on it found a crash on a line that had never run

The owner asked for a unified app — desktop or web — where batches can be built and changed
and where calculation fidelity is selectable with a sensible default chosen for them. This
record is the design, the three decisions inside it that were not obvious, and the two bugs
the quality gates caught on the way in.

**No physics changed.** `src/fermentation/` gains exactly one file, an empty `py.typed`
marker, and nothing else. What ships is `app/` (nine modules), `tests/test_app.py` (25
guards), the `ui` dependency group, and the toolchain changes that let the new code be held
to the same bar as the old.

### 1. Where it lives, and why not in the package

`app/` is a **top-level directory outside `src/`**, so it is not in the wheel. The engine's
install stays exactly what it was: four runtime dependencies and no interface code. Streamlit
and Plotly live in a `ui` dependency group, so a plain `uv sync` does not pull them; the app
needs `uv sync --group ui`.

The alternative — shipping it inside `fermentation` as an optional extra — was rejected on
one ground: the README's claim that this is a research engine with no interface is a claim
about what a consumer gets when they install it, and an optional extra that appears in the
package tree erodes it whether or not anyone enables the extra.

**Streamlit over a native window.** The delegation was "desktop or web". A native shell
(NiceGUI + pywebview) buys a real window and costs the layout time that went into the source
trail instead. The one real cost of the choice is named here so nobody rediscovers it: the
framework re-executes the whole page script on every widget change, which is what makes §3
below a live hazard rather than a theoretical one.

### 2. "Fidelity" is THREE axes, and only one of them is about being right

This is the part of the request that would have been easy to get wrong in a way that
contradicts prime directive 1. Three different things are called fidelity, and a single
quality slider spanning them would be exactly the silent blending the tier system exists to
forbid. They are separate controls, separately labelled:

| axis | control | what turning it up does |
|---|---|---|
| how carefully the maths is done | `method`/`rtol`/`atol`/`max_step` | converges to a fixed answer. Makes the run more like **this model**, never more like reality |
| how many points are stored | `t_eval` count | changes nothing about the answer. **Not** cosmetic on the ensemble path — members can only be aggregated on a shared grid, so the same count is threaded through both |
| what is being modelled | `oxidative` set, `strict` | the **only** axis here that can move correspondence with reality, and it is governed by tiers, not by a solver knob |

Two exclusions, both from `runtime/integrate.py`'s own docstring: **`RK45` appears in no
preset** (stiffness is guaranteed here, so an explicit method will crawl or fail; it is
reachable under "custom" only, labelled as a diagnostic), and **`max_step` is custom-only**
(BDF is adaptive, so a cap almost never changes the answer and always costs time).

**The default is demonstrated, not asserted.** "The app chooses a best variant by default"
is only honest if the default can be checked, so there is a button beside the control that
re-runs the batch one preset tighter and reports the largest relative change across the
headline quantities. It costs one extra integration (~1 s) and turns the preset from a claim
into a measurement. On all six starters the standard preset comes back converged at
1.5e-05 or better.

### 3. The one bug class this interface could produce silently — D-206 under a re-running framework

`CompiledScenario.run()` is not idempotent: an event's `reconfigure` mutates the Process set
in place and nothing puts it back, so a second `run()` starts with the first run's enables
live from t = 0. Under a framework that re-executes its script on every keystroke, *plus* a
cache that returns the same object on a hit, that is not a hazard to watch for — it is the
default outcome, and its symptom is a believable wrong curve with no error anywhere.

The rule, enforced in code and in a test: **`run_once` compiles fresh inside the cached call
every time, and the cache stores the finished, inert result.** Nothing in `app/` holds a live
`ProcessSet`; the mechanism metadata the source trail needs is copied out as plain data from
the public `active` view taken on either side of the run. Comparing those two views is also
what lets the page say which chemistry only started partway through, which is the honest
answer to "why is this line flat and then not".

`tests/test_app.py::test_each_run_starts_from_a_clean_scenario` is the guard. Its mutation
arm is a cache that keeps the compiled object: the aged-wine starter's mid-run switch set
would then be empty on the second run, and the final state would differ.

### 4. The reporting trap: an untouched slot reads `validated`

`ProcessSet.tier_of` combines with `min`, and the identity of a min over an empty list is the
**top** tier. So any variable no Process touches comes back from `tier_map` reading
`VALIDATED` — the one word nothing in this engine has earned. A naive interface would badge
an unhopped beer's bitterness, and browning in a run that never ages, as *confirmed against
measured data*.

`RunResult.touched_variables()` and `Readout.inert()` exist for that single reason. An
untouched quantity is reported as **inert** with no tier at all, and the copy says what that
means: it held its starting value throughout, which is not the same as being confirmed. The
guard is two-sided on purpose — it pins that the raw engine value really is `VALIDATED`, so
if that convention ever changes the test fails loudly instead of passing vacuously.

A second, smaller trap in the same family: **`Tier.SPECULATIVE` is the enum's zero and is
therefore falsy**, so `if tier:` silently reports the least confident tier as no tier at all.
Every check in `app/` is `is None`, and a test pins the falsiness so the discipline has a
stated reason.

### 5. Turning mypy on `app/` found two real bugs, one of them a crash

The obvious call was to leave the interface out of the type checker — `files = ["src",
"tests"]` did not cover a top-level `app/`, and its three dependencies ship no type
information. Including it instead cost one empty `src/fermentation/py.typed` (so the engine's
own types are visible from outside the package, which a strictly-typed library should ship
anyway) and one `ignore_missing_imports` override for `streamlit`/`plotly`/`pandas`, exactly
as `scipy` already had.

It paid for itself immediately:

- **`app/runner.py` read `ens.ensemble.sampled_names` on a bare `Ensemble`** — an
  `AttributeError` on the branch that warns when the uncertainty ranking is underdetermined.
  That line had never executed, so no amount of clicking would have found it before a user
  did.
- **`app/render.py` shadowed a `bool` with a `list[Readout]`** inside `series_figure` and
  then passed it on. Working by accident, and one edit away from not.

`app/` is therefore held to the same three gates as `src/`: `ruff check .`, `ruff format
--check`, `mypy`, and the suite. One documented exemption: `render.py` is excused C408,
because Plotly's figure spec is nested keyword objects and its own documentation is written
with `dict(...)`.

### 6. What the interface is FOR, stated so it does not drift

Plenty of software draws a fermentation curve. What this engine can do that they cannot is
name, for any point on a line, the chemistry that produced it, the published numbers that
chemistry used, the conditions each was measured under, its stated range, and therefore how
far the line may be believed. Every one of those facts is already required before a
parameter can load, so the source trail is assembly, not invention.

Two design commitments follow, and one correction the owner made mid-build:

- **Confidence is a visual channel, not a caption.** Line dash pattern is the tier, so it
  survives a screenshot. Solid is reserved for `validated` and is therefore never drawn; the
  legend says it is a standard being aimed at, not met. Untouched lines are long-dashed
  rather than solid, so the page contains no solid line at all — a scale whose top mark
  cannot be earned is more honest than one quietly rescaled to fit.
- **Known-weak readouts carry their warning onto the chart, every time.** Titratable acidity
  and bound SO₂ both have documented defects in this engine, and both warnings are attached
  to the readout rather than to a document, so they cannot be separated from the line.
- **The papers are reachable, not central** (owner, mid-build). The source trail was first
  built as a top-level tab, a peer of the run itself. It now lives in a collapsed expander at
  the foot of the run. Someone who wants a curve gets a curve; someone who wants the paper is
  two clicks away.

### 7. The copy is written for someone who has never read this repo

Also an owner correction, mid-build, with a worked example: *"Titratable acidity — Runs
BACKWARDS to real wine. The engine's by-product pool makes this rise ~3-4 g/L over a ferment
where a real one falls. Read the direction only, never the value."* That sentence uses an
internal term as if it were English (`by-product pool`), never says what titratable acidity
is, and — worse — its advice contradicts its own finding: if the direction is what is wrong,
the direction is exactly what must not be read.

Every user-facing string was rewritten. The same warning now reads: *"Trust the starting
value, not the finish. Total acidity is what a lab measures by titrating a sample. This model
counts everything the yeast makes as though it were acid, so the line climbs by roughly 3-4
g/L across a ferment. A real ferment holds steady or drifts slightly down. Day zero is sound;
after that it reads too high and moves the wrong way."*

The rule for anyone editing `app/`: no internal vocabulary in anything a user sees. Not
`Process`, `tier`, `state variable`, `compile`, `ensemble`, `solver tolerance`, `SRC`. The
short internal names survive in exactly one place — the source-trail selector — because that
is where they *are* the subject, and they are glossed on the spot.

### 8. Measured costs

Timed on the dev box, wine and beer starters, standard preset: **0.4-0.7 s to set up plus
0.3-1.1 s to integrate**, so a run computes in front of the user with no spinner worth
showing. The uncertainty ensemble is the exception at **~0.6 s per member**, which is why it
is an explicit button with the projected cost printed beside it and a UI default of 48
members rather than the engine's 200.

One consequence worth recording because it constrains the screen: a wine run samples **97
constants**, and the spread ranking is a regression of members on drawn parameters, so it is
underdetermined below ~98 members — about a minute. The page states the required count before
the button is pressed, and offers narrowing the draw to the constants one readout's own
chemistry reads, which is a different question and needs far fewer runs.

### 9. What is deliberately not here

- **No `validated` badge that can light up.** Not a limitation of the interface — a statement
  about the engine, drawn so it is visible.
- **No band on pH or any other quantity that is not one tracked variable times a fixed
  factor.** A percentile band computed on one input to the charge balance and relabelled
  "pH" would be a different quantity wearing pH's name. `render.bandable` refuses rather than
  draws.
- **No sensory/aroma screen of its own.** The aroma readouts appear on the run with the
  bluntest warning on the page, and nothing more is built until the honesty machinery around
  them has been exercised.
- **No server, no accounts, no persistence.** Saved runs live in the session; the written
  report is the durable artifact.

## D-262 — the console's four owner-reported faults, and the one that was not a drawing bug at all: an empty chart was the engine telling the truth about the batch and the page had no way to say so

**Corrects:** D-261 — the light theme was pinned on the argument that a thin dotted line loses its contrast on a dark ground. The constraint is real; the remedy was wrong. A second palette designed against near-black keeps the channel and gives back the choice.

The owner ran the console and reported four things: the colour chart draws nothing; there is
no dark mode; a lot of these curves want a log scale; and the plus/minus steppers fight back
— hold one down and the number jumps back to an older value. Three are interface work. The
first is not, and it is the one worth the record.

### 1. The empty chart was a correct answer with no sentence attached

"Colour and phenolics shows nothing" is four readouts — browning, free anthocyanin, polymeric
pigment, tannin — every one of them **inert** on the batch that was on screen. A white must
carries no pigment, so all four sit at exactly zero, and Plotly autoranges a set of identical
zeroes to **−1 … 1** on an axis labelled g/L. The page therefore drew half an axis of negative
concentrations under four invisible lines and said nothing. Nothing was broken. The engine had
answered "no chemistry in this run writes to any of these", the interface already *knew* that
— `Readout.inert` exists for it, and the legend was correctly drawing the pale long-dash — and
there was no place for the sentence that turns it into an answer.

Two fixes, deliberately at different levels:

- **Per axis**, a set of lines that is flat within the dust threshold gets the range 0 … 1
  instead of Plotly's −1 … 1. This is not cosmetic. On a chart labelled g/L or absorbance, a
  negative half-axis is a claim about the batch, and it is one no mechanism made.
- **Per chart**, `render.flat_group_panel` prints why it is empty. The trigger is inertness —
  the engine's own notion — and not flatness measured off the drawn series. That distinction
  is the whole design: the *oxygen* chart in the same run has three lines pinned at zero and
  acetaldehyde carrying the entire story, and "nothing here moves" would be false there.

**The trap inside the fix, found by running it.** The first wording blamed the missing
ingredient — "a white must has no colour compounds in it". Then the red wine starter, which
carries 0.5 g/L anthocyanin and 1.5 g/L tannin, produced *the same empty chart*: the pigment
chemistry only switches on once the wine is aging, and that starter never ages. The note as
written would have stood beside a sidebar displaying the very ingredient it said was absent.
Two batches reach one empty chart by opposite routes, so the panel now reports **flat at
zero** separately from **flat at the value it started from**, and the advice covers both
halves. `test_the_advice_on_the_empty_colour_chart_actually_fills_it` runs the batch the note
recommends and asserts every line it names is then driven — advice that is never executed
rots into decoration.

### 2. A palette is designed against a ground, so there are two of them

D-261 pinned `base = "light"` and wrote the reason into the config file: confidence here is
carried by line **weight** and dash pattern, and a 1.0 px pale long-dash is exactly what a
mismatched ground destroys. That reasoning is sound and it is why this could not be done by
flipping a switch. What was wrong was concluding that the ground must therefore be fixed. The
palette is eight hues taken from the subject; it wanted choosing **twice**, once against warm
near-white and once against warm near-black, with contrast at the *thinnest* weight as the
acceptance criterion rather than saturation.

`.streamlit/config.toml` now carries `[theme.light]` and `[theme.dark]`, which makes the
built-in Settings ▸ Appearance switch the whole page — verified in the browser before the
palette was written, because if that had not worked the design would have had to change to
CSS injection. `render.THEMES` supplies the matching chart ink and the sidebar's *Ink* control
follows the page by default. **`TIER_STYLE` is deliberately not per-theme.** A ground may
change a hue; it may never change what a dash means, or two screenshots of the same run would
disagree about how far a curve can be trusted. That invariant is a test, not a comment.

The written report had to be dealt with in the same breath. Its stylesheet flipped on
`prefers-color-scheme`, i.e. on the *reader's* machine, while its figures are drawn once and
baked in — so a dark report opened on a light desktop would have put dark charts on a white
page. The report now pins the ground the run was drawn in and travels with it.

### 3. A log axis has to be floored off the data, not off the solver's dust

The request is obvious and the implementation is not. Half the quantities here start at
exactly zero and several end at solver dust of order 1e-8. Left alone: Plotly autoranges to
that dust, so a 200 g/L ferment becomes a wiggle in the top decade of an eight-decade axis;
and it silently **drops** every non-positive point, so the sugar line appears to *stop* days
before the run ends. Neither failure announces itself — both produce a plausible picture.

So each axis is floored `LOG_DECADES` (six) below **its own peak**, and values under the floor
are drawn along the floor rather than dropped, with the true value carried in `customdata` so
the hover never reports the clamp. An axis on which nothing is positive is refused a log scale
outright rather than given a decade ruler over nothing. `render.log_scale_panel` then names
the lines this affected, because a reader who is not told will read a line lying along the
floor as a measurement of something very small.

### 4. The stepper that hands back an older number

The report was precise — hold plus down and it reverts — and the cause is two writers for one
value. Every number widget passed both `key=` and `value=`, with `value=` recomputed from
session state that is written at the *end* of the previous script run. Each click starts a
full re-run of the model (a second or two); a click landing inside that window is redrawn from
the older number the previous run had recorded. The widget was correct and the page overwrote
it.

The fix is both halves. The widget **key is now the only writer** — no `value=` anywhere in
the batch form, and `load_starter` seeds the keys directly. And the numbers live in a
`st.form`, so a stepper does not re-run anything until Apply; three rapid clicks now land as
three, verified in the browser against the run caption to confirm no re-run fired between
them. The extras chooser is deliberately left *outside* the form: inside, ticking a new
ingredient would have cost one Apply to reveal its box and a second to set it, which is a new
instance of the same complaint.

One adjacent defect fell out of the same reading. The temperature table is a *keyed*
`data_editor`, and a keyed editor stores edits, not data — handed a different starter's rows
under the same key, it replays the previous batch's edits on top of them. The key now carries
an epoch that is bumped whenever a starter or medium is loaded.

### What this cost, and what it did not

No physics changed and no parameter moved. `app/render.py` grows the two themes, the axis
logic and two panels; `Group` grows a `when_empty` sentence; `app/main.py` restructures the
form; `app/report.py` pins its ground. `tests/test_app.py` grows nine guards, of which the
two load-bearing ones are the theme invariant (a ground may not change a dash) and the
executable-advice test above.

## D-263 — three faults found by driving D-262's own work rather than reading it: a feature that undid its neighbour, the same two-writers bug on the one tab the sweep skipped, and a theme switch the server cannot see

**Corrects:** D-262 — the log-scale refusal returned before the flat-axis guard, so turning the log scale ON restored the exact empty-chart fault D-262 shipped to fix. Also corrects its claim that the charts "catch up" after a theme change by themselves; they do not.

D-262 shipped four interface fixes together and was verified on one tab, in one toggle
state. Each of the three faults below sat outside that box, and none of them would have
announced itself.

### 1. Two features in one commit, one silently undoing the other

`_axis_spec` handled two independent questions in one function: *should this axis be log*
and *is this axis degenerate*. The log refusal — correct in itself, an axis on which nothing
is positive gets no decade ruler — exited with an empty spec, which skipped the degenerate
guard below it. So the empty colour chart got its 0…1 range with the log toggle **off** and
Plotly's −1…1 back the moment it went **on**. The two halves of one commit, cancelling.

The guard did not catch it because it asserted `type != "log"`, which is true while the bug
is live: the axis had no type *and* no range. **A negative assertion cannot separate "the
right value" from "no value at all"**, and it passes vacuously whenever the path is skipped.
It now asserts `range[0] == 0.0` and loops over both toggle states.

### 2. The same fault as the steppers, on the tab nobody looked at

D-262's stepper diagnosis was that a keyed widget passing `value=` as well has two writers
and the stale one wins. Sweeping every call site afterwards found `st.text_input("Keep this
run as", value=scenario.name, key="save_as")` — the identical shape, on the compare tab.
`value=` seeds a keyed widget only at creation, so the box froze on the first batch's name
while the sidebar's own name field (which D-262 *had* fixed) moved on. Pressing "Keep it"
writes `saved[save_as] = result`, so a second batch would land on the first one's key,
overwrite the run it was going to be compared with, and offer one name where the user
believes there are two. Verified on screen before the fix: sidebar "Red wine, warm ferment
then malolactic", box still "White wine, cool and clean". Pre-existing since D-261.

The key now carries the run's name. The guard is source-level — nothing in `tests/test_app.py`
imports Streamlit — and pins the invariant rather than the syntax: the key expression varies
with the run name instead of being a constant.

### 3. A platform limit, measured rather than assumed

"Match the page" is the default, so the page's own theme control is the common path. It does
not work the way D-262's help text claimed. Streamlit 1.62 applies the new page CSS **without
re-running the script**, so `st.context.theme.type` is never re-read: switch to light and the
traces are still `#e8798f` on axis ink `#b8b1a6` after 2.5 s; press R and they become
`#7c1d3f` / `#55504a` at once. Both directions measured.

The server cannot detect this, because the script is not running when it happens. And the
stale state is not neutral — figures are drawn on a transparent ground, so a dark-inked
figure stranded on a white page loses its title to near-invisibility and drops the pale
"using the published values" line entirely. An opaque per-figure background would fix that
by making every chart a card that never blends into the page, which is a permanent cost for
a transient. So the honest remedy is the interface saying what happens: nothing re-runs until
you interact, the charts pick up the new ground at the next click or on R, and pinning Light
or Dark in the sidebar is itself a click and therefore lands immediately.

### What this says about the verification, not the code

All three came from *driving* the thing — a second toggle state, a second tab, a second
direction of one switch. None came from re-reading the diff. The pattern D-262 already
recorded (advice that is never executed rots into decoration) applies to a feature's own
acceptance: a fix verified in exactly the configuration it was written in has been checked
against its author's assumptions, not against the program.
## D-264 — the console started on exactly one machine: a report folder naming a drive nobody else has, a port collision that reads as "it did not work", and two probes that agreed with each other and with nothing else

**Corrects:** D-261 — the written report's destination was a constant naming a drive that exists on one machine, so *Write it* raised on every other one before writing a byte.

The question asked was whether someone who has never seen this project can start the console
and use it. Driving it as that person — rather than reading the code as its author — found
one shipped break, one barrier that had never been counted as part of the program, and two
faults in the *checking*, which are the part worth recording.

### 1. A destination that was true on one machine

`app/main.py` held a report folder written as an absolute path on drive `M:`, and `report.write`
creates the folder it is handed. On any machine without that drive the *Write it* button
raises before producing anything — the failure landing on the user least equipped to read a
traceback. It arrived by a route worth naming: the repo's own working rule says temporary
files go in a fixed folder on this machine, and that rule is about paths *the author* writes
while working. Applied to a constant inside software other people run, it ships the author's
filesystem to them.

`report.default_report_dir()` derives it instead: `FERMENTATION_CONSOLE_REPORTS` if set, else
`Documents/Fermentation Console` where `Documents` exists, else the same folder under home.
The success message now names the full path, because a file saved somewhere the user cannot
find has not really been saved.

The guard is on the class rather than on that constant. `test_no_shipped_interface_code_names_an_absolute_path`
scans every file under `app/` for a drive letter or a rooted unix path, in comments too — a
comment naming a false location is documenting the same falsehood. Re-inserting the old line
fails it.

### 2. Starting it was never counted as part of the program

The documented start is `uv sync --group ui` then `uv run streamlit run app/main.py`. That is
two commands, a terminal, and a tool the reader may not have — before anything of this project
is visible at all. `start-console.cmd` (double-click) and `start-console.sh` now wrap
`app/start_console.py`, which checks the interface dependencies, picks a port, and opens the
browser. Three constraints on it, each from a specific failure:

- **It installs nothing behind the user's back.** Missing `uv` gets one sentence and the
  address to get it. Downloading and running an installer on someone's machine is not a
  convenience the program is entitled to.
- **It runs headless and opens the browser itself.** Left to open its own browser, Streamlit
  stops and asks the terminal for an email address first. Nobody double-clicking an icon is
  watching a terminal, so that reads as a hang with no page.
- **It says everything in ASCII.** A Windows console draws an em dash happily; redirect the
  same output to a file and Python falls back to the machine's legacy codepage, where one dash
  raises `UnicodeEncodeError` — the launcher crashing while explaining itself. Measured here on
  an arrow, in this session, before it was written into the launcher.

Telemetry is off in `.streamlit/config.toml` rather than only on the launcher's command line,
so `app/README.md`'s "nothing is uploaded anywhere" is true however the console was started.
It was not, before.

### 3. What the page says before it says anything else

The first prose a first-time reader met was the trust panel — an epistemics disclaimer about a
model they had not yet been told they were looking at. The page now opens with one sentence
saying what it is, and a dismissible block saying where the batch lives, what *Apply and run*
does, and what a dash and a dot mean. Every composition field carries a sentence of its own:
"Assimilable nitrogen (YAN)" with no explanation is a number nobody outside a lab can set.

Those sentences describe what a quantity is and what a normal batch looks like. They do **not**
constrain the field. A range invented in the interface would be a number with no source behind
it, which is the one thing the parameter store forbids; the typical values are presentation,
and the engine still accepts what it accepts.

The three fidelity controls are now inside one collapsed section, and this is the place the
naive-user framing is most dangerous: the obvious move is to fold them into a single Quality
slider. They are three different things and only the third — which chemistry is included —
can move the answer towards or away from reality. Collapsed is not merged, and a widget inside
a closed expander is still created and still holds its value. The chemistry choice lost its own
expander (expanders cannot nest) and keeps its emphasis in words instead.

### 4. Two probes that agreed with each other and with nothing else

The launcher must not hand Streamlit a port something else is on. The reflex check is to bind
the port and see whether it raises. Run against a console that was *genuinely serving on 8613
at that moment*, it reported the port free. With `SO_REUSEADDR` on the probe, free again.
Windows hands a port over when the existing listener set that option, and Uvicorn sets it — so
on the platform this is most likely to be double-clicked on, a successful bind proves nothing
about whether anyone is there. A refused *connection* does, and that is what `port_is_free`
now asks.

Two probes agreeing is not corroboration when they share the assumption that is wrong. The
only reason this was caught is that the machine happened to have a real server running on a
known port while the probe was being written — the check was run against a *known* answer, not
against a hoped-for one.

Then the test written for it failed for a reason that was the test's own: a stand-in server
that listens with a backlog of one and never accepts fills that backlog on the first probe and
refuses the second, so the same busy port answered "busy" then "free". A test whose fixture is
not the thing it stands in for produces a red that is about the fixture. It accepts in a
thread now, as a real server does.

### What this beat says about verification

The three faults in §1–§3 are all invisible from inside the machine that wrote the code: the
drive exists here, the port was free here, the vocabulary is obvious here. D-263 recorded that
a fix verified in the configuration it was written in has been checked against its author's
assumptions rather than against the program. This is the same finding one layer out — a
program verified on the machine it was written on has been checked against that machine, and
"can a stranger start it" is not answerable by reading.
## D-265 — CI was not running what it said it ran: a type check against a machine with no console, a two-version matrix that only ever tested one version, and a port guard that could only pass on Windows

**Corrects:** D-264 — the stand-in server it added stops by closing a socket a thread is parked in `accept()` on, which is a Windows-only guarantee.

Eleven consecutive pushes were red, starting with D-261 and ending with the commit that
recorded the suite as green. Every one of them died in the type check, which sits before the
test step — so no run since D-260 had executed a single test, and the "2131 + 6 xfail in
397 s" in D-264 was measured here and nowhere else. Three faults, nested: the second was
hidden by the first, the third by the second. Each was invisible until the one above it was
lifted.

### §1 The type checker was reading the console with the console's libraries absent

The engine is deliberately a four-dependency research library, so `streamlit` and `plotly`
live behind their own `ui` dependency group and a plain `uv sync` does not install them. But
mypy is configured `files = ["src", "tests", "app"]` and checks the interface regardless. With
the library missing, `st.stop()` loses its `NoReturn` annotation — and that annotation is the
*only* thing telling the checker that the code below a missing-scenario guard is unreachable.
Every narrowing downstream of one collapsed at once: 44 errors, of the form "Item None of
Scenario | None has no attribute", on code that is correct.

The shape worth keeping: a strict checker run against a partial environment does not report
"I am missing a package". It reports the *consequences* of missing it, in the vocabulary of
the code under test, at 44 sites that all look like real defects. Nothing in that output names
the cause. The tell was that the same command was green on the machine that wrote the code —
a green local run and a red CI run of *the same checker* is a statement about the environment,
never about the code.

Reproduced before fixing, in a throwaway environment pointed at by `UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT` so
the working `.venv` was untouched: `uv sync` alone gives the 44 errors, `uv sync --group ui`
gives "no issues found in 161 source files".

### §2 The two-version matrix had never tested two versions

Installing the group turned 3.14 green through the type check. 3.13 stayed red, and its
install log says why in three lines. `uv sync --python 3.13` reported "Using CPython 3.13.15"
and installed streamlit and plotly. The next step, a bare `uv run ruff check .`, reported
"Using CPython 3.14.7", "Removed virtual environment at: .venv", and reinstalled 27 packages —
the default groups only.

A bare `uv run` does not inherit the interpreter its sync used. It takes the newest one it can
find, and where that differs from the environment on disk it *deletes that environment and
rebuilds it*. So the ui group was thrown away before mypy ran, which is the local fault. The
one that matters is the other one: every step after the sync had been running 3.14 on the job
labelled 3.13, for the entire life of the matrix. **No test in this repo had ever executed on
Python 3.13.** `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` has said "CI runs all four on Python 3.13 and 3.14"
throughout; the sentence became true at this commit and not before.

`--python` therefore goes on all five `uv run` steps rather than the sync alone — any single
unpinned step rebuilds the environment and poisons every step after it — and `--group ui` goes
on all five too, so that no step can be the one that drops it. **Those five flag pairs are not
boilerplate.** Deleting them as redundant restores the bug silently, and the failure it
restores does not look like a workflow fault; it looks like the console failing to type-check.

The general form: a CI matrix asserts that it varies something. Nothing in a green run
verifies that it did. The evidence here was one line — "Removed virtual environment" — in a
step whose *output* was "All checks passed!".

### §3 The port guard could only ever pass on the operating system it was written on

With §1 and §2 fixed, the test step ran for the first time since D-260: 2131 tests, one
failure. D-264's own guard, on its last line — the one asserting the port is free again once
the stand-in server is closed.

Closing a file descriptor that another thread is blocked in `accept()` on is undefined by
POSIX. Windows aborts the pending accept immediately, so the socket really is gone. Linux may
leave the thread parked in the kernel, and the parked accept holds the listening socket open —
so the port goes on serving after `close()`, and the final probe is *right* to call it busy.
`join(timeout=2)` then gives up silently and the test never looks at the result, so a teardown
that did not happen surfaces as a probe that does not work.

Measured rather than argued: the teardown was lifted into a standalone harness and run under
CPU load on WSL, which is the CI condition. **7 failures in 60 rounds, and the accept thread
was still alive in exactly those 7** — the free-check failed if and only if the thread had not
stopped. The same harness with the socket given a 0.1 s timeout, the loop watching an
`Event`, and the join asserted: **0 in 60**, on Linux and on Windows.

The three assertions are unchanged — busy probes busy, `choose_port` refuses it, the port
probes free once the server is really gone — and one assertion was added that fails the test
if the stand-in never stopped. That addition is the actual repair. The unchecked `join` was
the defect; a teardown that ignores whether it worked will rot back to this the moment the
timing changes.

### What this beat says about verification

D-264 closed on: a program verified on the machine it was written on has been checked against
that machine. This is the same finding two layers further out, and the layers are worth naming
separately.

- **The environment.** §1: a checker run against a subset of the dependencies reports defects
  in the code, not in the environment. A tool that is green here and red there is describing
  the *there*.
- **The platform.** §3: a green test proves the property holds on the operating system that
  ran it. D-264's docstring already said "the failure this pins is a Windows one" — the author
  knew the platform mattered for what the test *pins*, and the platform assumption that
  actually broke was in the teardown, which nobody thinks of as part of the test.
- **The harness itself.** §2 is the one with no analogue in the earlier records. §1 and §3 are
  faults in code that CI correctly reported. §2 is a fault in *CI*, which reports nothing,
  because a harness that silently does less than it claims still comes back green. Eleven red
  runs were needed to expose a bug that a hundred green ones would have concealed — the matrix
  was only caught because something else forced its two jobs to disagree.

The tests are not the thing that establishes a claim. The thing that ran them is, and it makes
its own claims, which are unverified by default.

## D-266 — the JOINT fusel repair, run for the first time: D-257's blend and D-259/D-260's growth-anchored sink were each refused on a ground the other removes, and the pair clears D-257's blocker, keeps the blend's timing, lands Rollero's tracer — and is a different point on D-260's line, not an escape from it

**Corrects:** D-257 — §2's "any repair for D-256's temporal defect must slow production in the growth window, so any repair trips this [the phenylalanine stranding]. It is not a property of the blend." That generalisation was measured under the shipped sink only. ### 2. The harness reproduces the archive before it measures anything

The `blend` arm is D-257's repair rebuilt as a patch on the bindings the code reads —
`byproducts.fusel_rate_shape` for production and its sugar draw, `ehrlich_draws` in **two**
modules for attribution (`precursor_fates` imports it by value, D-256's trap) — and reads
D-257's own numbers: 36.5 / 48.4 / 56.9 % of isoamyl at nitrogen-gate closure on Rollero's
three musts, 172.37 mg/L at the D-112 anchor, 72.86 % of phenylalanine stranded on the D-104
fixture. The `growth` arm is D-260's counterfactual with growth's modifiers attached and reads
27.582 % / 5.900 %. The `shipped` arm reads 81.5 % / 1.507 % / 2123.3 µM. Every quadrature
closure in every arm is 1.0000, asserted in the fixture (D-259 §7's discipline).

**The positive control on the patch itself:** at `f = 1` with the five `k` unscaled, the joint
machinery reproduces the growth arm to `rel 1e-6` on every split and on isoamyl. So the patch
reaches the code and does nothing it was not asked to — D-257's form is isolable by a parameter,
as D-257 claimed.

### 3. THE BLOCKER CLEARS — and D-257 §2's generalisation does not survive

D-257 reverted the repair because slowing production stranded the must's phenylalanine, and
wrote that *any* repair for the temporal defect trips it. Under the growth-anchored sink the
same repair — same `f`, same `k` rescale, same attribution scaling — leaves **0.00006 %** of
the D-104 fixture's phenylalanine and **0.000004 %** of Crépin's, from the blend-alone arm's
72.9 % and 56.2 %. Final biomass is within 2 % across all four arms, so the change is the
sink's and not the ferment's. D-259 §6 had measured this within-fixture under the `k` rescale
alone; this is the measurement with production actually slowed.

### 4. The blend moves the point along D-260's line and does not move the line

D-260's identity `tracer = (1 − split) · consumed / isoamyl` binds because the leucine pool
empties whatever draws it and isoamyl is inert under a sink swap. Both invariances hold in all
four arms here. What the blend does is cut the Ehrlich draw (×0.79 gated, ×0.4033 on `k`), so
under the growth sink the lump absorbs the residue:

| Crépin's must, mid composition | shipped | blend | growth | joint |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| leucine split, % | 81.5 (imposed) | 81.5 (imposed) | 27.6 | **54.5** (46.0-61.5 across the bracket) |
| leucine tracer, % of isoamyl | 1.507 | 1.472 | 5.900 | **3.617** (4.29-3.06) |
| isoamyl, µM | 2123 | 2174 | 2123 | **2177** |

The pre-registered mechanism said the split gain would be paid on the tracer. **It is not,
because the split stops at 54.5 % and the line then leaves 3.6 % for the tracer** — inside
Rollero's 3.4-8.2 % where the shipped model reads 1.5 %. And the line itself is the same line:
isoamyl on this must moves 2123 → 2177 µM, because the blend is level-preserved at the Wang
anchor by construction and Crépin's 28 °C must lands at the same total. The joint-satisfaction
ceiling (≤ 1170 µM at Crépin's 77 %) is exactly where D-260 §6 left it; the joint arm is a
third point on the line, 1.4× under Crépin where the growth arm was 2.8× under. **D-260's
"neither is the other's repair" survives, sharpened: nor is the pair.**

### 5. What the pair costs, and neither half could have shown it

* **The three precursors the shipped sink imposes.** `f_non_ehrlich_isoleucine/valine/threonine`

  every composition edge). The end inversion D-259 found survives (leucine lowest, threonine

  within a point of each other. Phenylalanine reads 99.6 % against the sourced 0.975, just
  above D-259's 96-99.5 window.
* **The growth sink ALONE breaks the sourced propanol floor.** Un-capped by `f`, threonine's
  Ehrlich draw runs and propanol reads **71.4 %** de novo against the 80 % floor D-244 asserted
  and D-248 cleared; the blend's cut brings the pair back to 87.5 %, beside the shipped 87.8 %.
  D-259/D-260 never scored propanol, so the growth sink's refusal was standing on the wrong
  ground — the propanol floor refuses it on its own, and the pair relieves it.
* **On Rollero's own musts the leucine tracer brackets the enrichment and over-shoots the
  amount.** 1.78 / 5.44 / 8.33 % against Table S2's 3.4-3.5 / 4.2-4.7 / 6.8-8.2 %: under, over,

  Scored apart from the total, the labelled amount is **101 and 171 µM against 55-64 and 65-70**,

  Two errors cancelling, the D-256 shape.
* **Valine's tracer moves the wrong way**: 0.87 / 2.15 / 2.85 % against Table S1's 2.1-2.3 /
  3.4-4.0 / 5.3-5.4, below the shipped arm's own under-reading, because the blend makes most

### 6. What the numbers decide, and what they leave to the owner

Per axis, against the shipped model, the joint arm is closer to reality on: the timing of
higher-alcohol production (100 % at gate closure → 37-57 % vs 42-54), the isoamyl nitrogen
response (2.27× → 1.30× vs 0.76×), the isoamyl level at SM250 and SM425 (1.55× / 3.0× → 1.38× /
2.25× Rollero's), phenylalanine consumption, and the leucine tracer on Crépin's must. It is
further on: the isoamyl level at SM70 (1.00× → 1.31×), the isoleucine/valine/threonine splits
(exact by construction → 15-43 points over), and valine's tracer. It reaches neither Crépin's
leucine split nor a joint satisfaction of the two papers, and what still binds is the isoamyl
level the Wang 172 mg/L real-wine anchor sets against synthetic-medium totals — D-260 §6's
commensurability question, now shown invariant to both repairs.

That is a fork between sourced static splits that are exact by construction and emergent ones
that are right on new axes and wrong on old ones, off a yeast protein composition recorded
nowhere (D-259 §2). **"Closer to reality decides" needs one direction; this has two. Not
shipped; the owner's call, now priced on every axis at once.**

### 8. Two pieces of structure this beat needed and the project did not have

* **`docs/OPEN.md`, generated by `tools/gen_open_ledger.py`.** The project had no live answer to
  "what is scientifically open": the archive is 37k append-only lines, the plans are frozen, the
  memory is agent-only, and this beat itself began by re-deriving from four records what two
  markers could have said. The ledger is derived from the only two machine-checkable signals —
  every `xfail`/`skip` marker under `tests/` and every open `Flags:` pair — and reads no prose,
  because a record's own "what stays open" is a breadcrumb list (D-156's still named a withdrawn
  item). It grows a retirement marker, `**Unflags:** D-F [on D-T] — clause`, validated (must
  postdate D-F, D-F must declare the flag) so the correction map can finally close a flag without
  editing history. `--check` in CI, `tests/test_open_ledger.py` beside it.
* **Six shipped markers were invisible to the index.** `**Flags:** D-164 §6`, `D-165 §6`,
  `D-166 §2`, `D-167 §5`, `**Corrects:** D-127/D-176` (D-179), `**Corrects:** D-192 §9` (D-194)
  did not match the marker grammar and had carried no weight in the correction map for up to
  a hundred records. The ledger generator found them by counting marker-shaped lines the grammar
  rejected; the grammar now admits a section and a `/`, and the four self-flags (a record
  flagging a section of itself as identified-not-shipped) are admitted as open items while a
  self-`Corrects` or self-`Unflags` stays refused. The index gains six back-edges; the ledger
  reads 68 open flags on 48 records and 6 strict xfails.

### 1. No pre-registration, and the expectation that was wrong

A transcription has no arm to blind, so nothing was registered. The one honest prediction this
beat began with — that the bracket was an author estimate no source would reach, and that the
beat would end by attaching a citation to numbers that stayed put — **was wrong twice**: the
protein half is corroborated at all three of its edges (§3), and the residue half is contradicted
at all five of its high edges (§5).

### 2. Where the search went, because "blocked on external sourcing" has been wrong ten times

The corpus sweep is listed in the receipts. It covered the 42 extracted `manual_sources` texts
and the 24 textbook extractions; the two PDFs in the repo that have **no text extraction and so
had never been inside any grep** (they are Coleman, Fish & Block 2007 — already this engine's
growth anchor — and Moimenta *et al.* 2025; neither carries a composition); and
`d255-rollero-medium/`, the folder where D-256's leucine tracer had already sat unread, whose
supplement turns out to hold a **must** composition and not a biomass one.

**The eleventh instance did not happen: this one really was not in the repo.** That is worth
recording as its own result. The shape has been wrong ten times, and what makes "externally
sourced" a finding rather than an excuse is being able to say which places were checked.

### 3. The protein fraction of dry weight — three anchors, and D-259's bracket survives

40-45 % from the *Concise Encyclopedia*'s wine yeast (**in this repo**, and a grep away all
along), 42 % from van Gulik & Heijnen 1995 Table I after Verduyn — the standard stoichiometric
yeast biomass — and ~50 % from an *Understanding Wine Chemistry* chapter note, which is the
weakest of the three and is labelled so in the receipts because it reasons from a **bread-yeast
packet's nutrition label**. D-259's `{0.40, 0.45, 0.50}` brackets all three and is not moved.

### 4. The residue composition, and why the conversion is the whole finding

**Lange HC, Heijnen JJ (2001), *Biotechnol Bioeng* 75(3):334-344, Table IV p.339 — "Amino acid
composition of the protein as measured (mol %)"**, glucose-limited chemostat *S. cerevisiae*.
The paper states the relative abundance did not vary between cultures, which is what licenses
carrying a chemostat composition to a fermenting must. Transcribed verbatim from the table image
now in `docs/receipts/d267-yeast-protein-composition/`; its 19 rows sum to **100.02** mol %,
which is the only check an image transcription admits and is a guard.

The table is a **mole** composition; the constant is a **mass** one. Protein mass is the sum of
**residue** masses, but `_GrowthAnchoredFates` subtracts its draw from the **free** amino-acid
pool, and the engine's `MOLAR_MASS` is the free acid — leucine 131.175, not the residue's
113.160. That is checked against `src/` in a guard rather than asserted here, and it comes back
with zero mismatches on all five. So a `w_i` in residue grams removes too few grams from the
pool, by exactly the peptide-bond water: the free-acid shares sum to **116.53** per 100 g of
protein where the residue shares sum to 100.00.

**This is a units fork, not a band** (D-209). One reading ships — the free-acid frame, because
it is not a judgement about the literature but about this model's own arithmetic — and the other
is pinned beside it as the named loser so no later beat crosses the two into a "band" whose
whole spread is the fork.

### 5. THE FINDING: in the frame the draw uses, every precursor is above the bracket

g per 100 g protein, against D-259's lo/mid/hi:

| | bracket | residue frame | | **free-acid frame** | | over `hi` | over `mid` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| leucine | 6.0 / 7.5 / 9.0 | 8.315 | inside | **9.639** | **above hi** | 1.071x | 1.285x |
| isoleucine | 4.0 / 5.0 / 6.0 | 6.115 | above hi | **7.088** | **above hi** | 1.181x | 1.418x |
| valine | 4.5 / 5.5 / 6.5 | 6.666 | above hi | **7.878** | **above hi** | 1.212x | 1.432x |
| threonine | 4.0 / 5.0 / 6.0 | 5.166 | inside | **6.087** | **above hi** | 1.015x | 1.217x |
| phenylalanine | 3.5 / 4.5 / 5.5 | 5.077 | inside | **5.698** | **above hi** | 1.036x | 1.266x |

The two frames do not even agree about *which* edges break — the residue frame contradicts only
isoleucine and valine — which is why the fork had to be decided rather than averaged.

**The consequence, stated and not acted on.** A larger `w_i` draws more precursor into the lump,
so the direction is unambiguous: every growth-anchored number in D-259, D-260 and D-266 was
computed at a per-precursor draw **21.7-43.2 % below** what the only measured composition plus the
engine's own molar masses imply, and the `mid` composition those records quote as their headline
is the furthest from it. **D-260's 27.58 % leucine split and D-266's joint 54.50 % are low
estimates**, and D-266 §6's per-axis fork was priced at a composition the source does not
support. Nothing is re-measured here, because re-pricing those arms *is* the owner-gated build.

### 6. A second frame that does NOT reconcile, reported because it was checked

"40-45 % protein **based on N x 6.25**" is a crude-protein convention: it asserts total nitrogen
of 6.4-7.2 % of dry weight. The *Understanding Wine Chemistry* note's own arithmetic (protein is
one-sixth nitrogen, protein is ~50 % of dry weight) asserts 8.3 %. The engine ships
`biomass_N_fraction` = **0.114** g N/g cell, from Roels' generic CH1.8O0.5N0.2 — **1.6-1.8x the
nitrogen those two wine-yeast statements imply** — and running the convention the other way
turns 0.114 into a 71 % crude-protein cell, far above every anchor in §3.

Nothing is done with this and it carries no flag: it is not an agreed reversal, it touches the
shipped nitrogen budget rather than a test constant, and one of its two ends is a bread-yeast
label. It is recorded so the next beat reaching for either number knows the pair does not close.

### 7. What ships

Six guards appended to `tests/test_precursor_fates.py`, none of which runs the model: the mol %
closure and row count; the frame claim checked against the engine's own `MOLAR_MASS`, including
that free minus residue is exactly one water; the finding itself, pinned as ratios to the
bracket's own edges so it survives a re-derivation; the losing frame pinned beside it, asserting
that it breaches **exactly** isoleucine and valine; the protein-fraction anchors, asserting each
lies inside 0.40-0.50 and that the two extremes are reached; and a guard on the bracket literal
itself, whose failure message says that changing it means taking the flagged build and retiring
this record's flag rather than updating a number.

Receipts: `docs/receipts/d267-yeast-protein-composition/` — `FINDINGS.md`, `convert.py`,
`findings.json`, `lange_heijnen_2001_tableIV.png`.

### 8. What stays open

* The repair is the owner's, priced in §5. Taking it means moving five test constants and
  re-measuring every growth-anchored arm in D-259, D-260 and D-266 — it does not change `src/`,
  but it changes what those three records report, which is why it is flagged and not shipped.
* Lange & Heijnen's composition is a glucose-limited chemostat, not a fermenting must. The
  paper's own "did not vary between cultures" is what carries it across, and that is a stability
  claim about their cultures, not about wine.
* §6's nitrogen-frame mismatch — the engine's 0.114 g N/g cell against the 6.4-8.3 % the two
  wine-yeast protein statements imply — is untouched and belongs to whatever beat next opens the
  nitrogen budget.

### 2. The design decided before measuring: derived, not re-typed

`w_i(edge) = protein_fraction[edge] × free_acid_share[species] / 100`, where the share is read
out of the Table IV transcription D-267 already guards, through `_lange_heijnen_shares("free")`.
**No second literal is typed.** The only hand-entered numbers on this path stay Table IV's own
19 rows, which have a mole-closure guard, and the conversion, which has a frame guard against
the engine's `MOLAR_MASS`. The residue half stops being a bracket because it is a measurement;
what survives as a bracket is the protein fraction of dry weight, `{0.40, 0.45, 0.50}`,

**inverted rather than deleted**: it asserted that the literal had not been silently edited, and
now asserts that the weights really are derived from the source and that the superseded literal
is off the path a model run reads. A revert is as much an archive event as taking it was.

### 3. The reproduction that licenses every number below

The superseded composition is not only kept as a comment — it is kept as **live arms**. On it,

and in the two guards that report the new numbers, so the re-pricing is *auditable* rather than

phenylalanine 97.2-98.5 → 98.3-98.6. D-260's corrected (post-modifier) leucine bracket:
21.3-33.7 → **30.3-35.2 %**.

### 5. THE FINDING: D-266's headline is retracted by its own composition

D-266 pre-registered that the joint repair would push the leucine tracer below Rollero's 3.4 %
floor, measured 3.617 %, and **scored its own prediction wrong**. The identity that binds it is
D-260's: `tracer = (1 − split) · consumed / isoamyl`, with the pool emptied whatever draws it and
isoamyl inert under a sink change. Raising every weight raises the split, so the tracer must fall.

| joint arm | leucine split | leucine tracer | against Rollero 3.4-8.2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| stated composition (D-266) | 54.50 % | 3.617 % | inside |
| sourced, **lo** | 57.77 % | **3.356 %** | below the floor |
| sourced, **mid** | **60.61 %** | **3.131 %** | below the floor |
| sourced, **hi** | 63.09 % | **2.934 %** | below the floor |

**The whole of what is left of the bracket is below the floor.** The pre-registered mechanism was
right; what was wrong was the composition it had been priced at. The denominator does not move
(isoamyl 2176.6 µM in every joint arm against the shipped 2123.5 — the blend is level-preserved
at the Wang anchor by construction), so this is a different point on D-260's line and not an
escape from it. **The joint arm now misses BOTH of the two leucine observables it was offered as
satisfying one of**, and D-266 §6's "closer to reality needs one direction; this has two" is
re-priced: the direction that made the fork two-sided was this one.

### 6. The two dials, deliberately treated differently

`_D260_MATCHED_F` is a **control**, defined as the shipped-form `f` that matches the
growth-anchored split — and the shipped form's realised split is exactly `f`, so it is that split
read off the run. 0.174 → **0.2135**, re-derived.

**Its two asserts are not both evidence, and the record should not read them as if they were.**
The split-agreement assert (the two arms within 0.5 points; it reads 0.001) compares a hardcoded
literal against the number that literal was set from — it says nothing about the mechanisms. What
it *is* is a **staleness tripwire on the literal**, and this beat is the one that made it fire:
move the composition without re-deriving `f` and the two arms separate by four points. The
load-bearing assert is the other one — the two arms' **tracers** agreeing to 1.0001x at a matched
split, which has teeth because they run different mechanisms, and which is the whole of D-260 §4's
claim that the tracer tracks the split rather than the mechanism.

`_D260_LAMBDA` is a **dial priced at a number** and is **left at 5.0**. What it buys is
re-reported instead, and that produced the D-260 correction above: on the stated composition λ=5
landed the split at 73.29 %, below Crépin's floor, while D-260's prose said it landed in her band
— the guard was pinned at 70, four points under her floor, so neither failed. On the sourced
composition the same λ lands **77.83 %**, genuinely inside 77-86, the crossing sits at λ≈4.8, and
the guard is re-pinned against her floor so the two can no longer disagree. **The price of the
numerator lever fell; that is a finding, and retuning λ to keep a window green would have erased
it.**

### 7. What survives the re-pricing

* **The refusal.** Corrected leucine tops out at 35.22 % against Crépin's 77-86 %.
* **D-259's order correction.** Isoleucine still above valine (32.97 vs 32.12 at the middle); the
  margin narrows from 1.0 to 0.9 points.
* **D-259's positive finding.** Phenylalanine lands 98.25-98.59 % against its sourced 97.5 %, and
  the control that stops it being an artefact of supply limitation still holds with 75 points to
  spare (leucine 19.4-23.2 %).
* **D-260's two conclusions.** D-104's 20.9 % is still below the corrected low edge — by 9.4
  points now rather than 0.4 — and the corrected high edge is still far under Crépin's floor.
* **D-266's blocker clearance and its ledgers.** The joint arm still strands no phenylalanine
  (0.0000 %), carbon and nitrogen still close to zero relative drift, net dS/dt never positive.

### 8. The costs, and the one axis that improves without being a win

The three splits Crépin's own numbers are imposed on over-shoot **further**: isoleucine
66.2 → 73.5, valine 65.2 → 73.0, threonine 81.2 → 84.0, against her 51 / 41 / 38. The D-117
sparing-credit refund rises 0.236 → **0.276x** growth's draw (it scales with the draw), against
the shipped 0.584x and the hard 1.0. Propanol's de-novo share on the growth-alone arm rises
0.714 → 0.746, still under the sourced 0.80 floor, and the joint arm still restores it
(0.875 → 0.894 beside the shipped 0.878).

Rollero's 13C-leucine enrichment is the one axis that moves **toward** the source: 1.78 / 5.44 /
8.33 → **1.54 / 4.69 / 7.18 %** against Table S2's 3.4-3.5 / 4.2-4.7 / 6.8-8.2, so two of three
go from outside the band to inside it. **It is not agreement.** Scored apart from the total it is
divided by, the labelled *amount* is 86.7 µM against his 55.2-64.2 at SM250 (1.35x) and 147.3
against 65.0-70.3 at SM425 (2.10x), while the total is ~2x his. Two errors cancelling more
closely than before, which makes the ratio more misleading, not less. Valine's tracer stays wrong
in the same direction and moves further out.

### 9. A guard this beat got wrong, and the suite caught it

The first draft of the receipts claimed the joint arm's gate-closure fraction had moved to **1.13
points** from the blend's at SM425 and **widened that guard's bound from 1.0 to 1.5** to admit it.
Both were wrong. The 1.13 came from comparing the joint arm measured here against D-257's
*recorded* blend number instead of against the blend arm measured in the same run. The real gap
is 0.107 / 0.110 / 0.114 points — flat, and unchanged by a composition change that moves the
Crépin splits by 6-11 points. The bound is back at 1.0 and now carries a second assert pinning
the gap under 0.25, four times tighter than before this beat touched it.

Recorded because the failure mode is the one the project keeps meeting from the other side: a
number read against a *published* value rather than against the arm beside it in the same run.
The widened bound would have shipped silently; the extra assert I wrote to "pin the shape" is
what failed. [[feedback-a-gap-needs-both-sides-from-the-same-run]]

Also worth its own line, because a passing guard says nothing about its margin: the growth arm's
SM70 leucine enrichment reads **3.5011 %** against Table S2's 3.5 % ceiling. "The growth arm alone
is over Rollero's ceiling on all three musts" is now carried at SM70 by one thousandth of a point.

### 10. What ships

`tests/test_precursor_fates.py`: the weights derive from the transcription; the superseded
bracket and a `_d259_superseded_weights` helper; D-267's tripwire inverted; two new guards (the
per-precursor per-edge re-pricing ratios, and the inverted tripwire's two-way check); five
existing guards re-pinned with the reproduction arms beside the live ones.
`tests/test_fusel_joint_repair.py`: `_crepin_arm` and `_install_growth_sink` take explicit
weights; `growth_superseded` and `joint_superseded` arms; six guards re-pinned, one of them
inverted (the tracer band).

Receipts: `docs/receipts/d268-sourced-composition-repricing/` — `PREREGISTRATION.md`,
`FINDINGS.md`, `probe.py`, `lambda_sweep.py`, `findings.json`.

### 11. What stays open

* **The owner-gated build D-266 §9 reserved is now priced on a sourced composition, and its
  shape has changed.** It was offered as a fork with two directions — the joint repair being
  right on new axes and wrong on old ones. On the sourced composition it is wrong on both leucine
  observables, further out on the three imposed splits, and closer only on an enrichment whose
  numerator is 1.4-2.1x the source's. That is one direction, not two. The call is still the
  owner's; what changed is that "closer to reality decides" now has something to decide with.
* Lange & Heijnen's composition is still a glucose-limited chemostat carried to a fermenting must
  on the paper's own "did not vary between cultures" (D-267 §8). Nothing here strengthens that.
* D-267 §6's nitrogen-frame mismatch — the engine's 0.114 g N/g cell against the 6.4-8.3 % two
  wine-yeast protein statements imply — is untouched, and is the only part of D-267 this record
  does not close.
